Senator Bailey, Representative Mathieson, and distinguished members of the Joint Standing
Committee on Health Coverage, Insurance and Financial Services: I am Senator Rick
Bennett of Oxford, and I have the honor of serving the people of 14 towns in western Maine
in the Senate. I am pleased present LD 23, "An Act to Extend the Period of Time a Dentist May Operate the Practice of a Deceased or Incapacitated Dentist."
I brought this bill forward on behalf of my constituent, Chiye Harper of Fryeburg. Chiye and
her husband, Michael Harper, owned and operated the Fryeburg Dental Center. Michael was the licensed dentist and Chiye ran the books and administrative side of the practice. Tragically, last January, Michael passed away at the age of 46. His death hit the community hard. Last year, the Legislature recognized his life of service as a missionary and his service
in the US Army with a sentiment in memoriam.
Under current law, the legal guardian or personal representative of a deceased or incapacitated dentist has 24 months to operate the practice. That gives Ms. Harper about a year to sell or enter into a partnership with another dentist. Frankly, she needs more time to get organized and go through with the process, especially after such a devastating loss. It is not easy to manage a bustling dental practice, sell a business, and raise four children all alone, particularly while grief-stricken. All Ms. Harper is asking of us is a little more time.
Fryeburg Dental Center has 22 employees and provides services for more than 4,000 patients. There is also a second practice, run by Chiye, right next door which is specifically for Maine Care Dental patients. This practice serves people all over Maine and gives
expedited services to individuals under Maine Care. We all know about how important
dentists are and that there is currently a shortage in many parts of the state.
Thank you for your time and consideration today. I urge you to vote "ought to pass" on this
bill.

Testimony of the Maine Dental Association before the Health Coverage, insurance and Financial Services Committee
LD 23 An Act to Extend the Period of Time a Dentist May Operate the Practice of a Deceased
or incapacitated Dentist
ln Support Public Hearing: Tuesday, January 28, 2025
Senator Bailey, Representative Mathieson and Distinguished Members of the Health Coverage,
Insurance and Financial Services Committee:
I am Therese Cahill and I serve as Executive Director ofthe Maine Dental Association. The MDA is a
statewide association dedicated to advancing excellence in dentistry. Unfortunately, I am unable to attend today's Public Hearing as l am out of state.
The MDA represents 85% of the dentists in Maine; there are approximately 775 practicing and retired
dentists who are active members of the association.
On behalf ofthe Maine Dental Association, l am respectfully providing testimony in support of LD 23 An Act to Increase the Period of Time a Dentist May Operate the Practice of a Deceased or incapacitated
Dentist.
Notable here is the fact that across the country, the average number of dentists per capita is 60.4%; in Maine, the average number of dentists per capita is 54.5%. Without question, the closure of one practice will negatively impact hundreds of patients.
Like so many professions across our State, our members continue to face critical staffing shortages. Most practicing dentists are small business owners who, often along with family members, manage all aspects of operation of their dental office. When the dentist owner dies or becomes incapacitated, the small business needs to continue to function while the family and staff make their way through the
personal process of grief. By allowing additional time to get the office's affairs in order to prepare the business to be sold, Maine would be honoring the family's process, keep a small business open, support
the employment of staff, and continue to serve the often small communities who would struggle to find
dental care due to an office closure. We're all aware that Maine, despite passage ofan adult Medicaid dental benefit and a substantial increase to dental fees, continues to struggle with sufficient access to
care.

For your information l have included 2 graphics published by the American Dental Association outlining Maine Dentist Demographics (54.5 per 100,000) as well US Dentist Demographics (60.4 per 100,000).
Should you have any questions, please don't hesitate to contact me (tcahillgv>meclenta�.org).
Thank you for your time and attention.

The issue of a dentist shortage is a concern that should not be overlooked. As someone who has personally experienced long wait times for appointments and limited availability, I understand the frustration that comes with trying to access dental care in a timely manner.
The shortage of dentists not only impacts individual patients but also puts a strain on the overall healthcare system. Many people are forced to go without essential dental treatments due to the lack of availability, which can have serious implications for their oral health and overall well-being.
It is imperative that action is taken to address this shortage and ensure that everyone has access to quality dental care when they need it. Whether through increasing funding for dental schools, incentivizing more students to pursue careers in dentistry, or expanding telehealth options, creative solutions are needed to tackle this pressing issue.
In conclusion, the dentist shortage is a problem that requires attention and action. By coming together to address this issue, we can ensure that everyone has access to the dental care they need to maintain a healthy smile.
